# 08-fresco — sources

Back-test entry `08-fresco.yaml`: Fresco, the AI scribe for construction superintendents (YC Fall 2024).
Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's choice" marks the
smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Fresco (YC F24), 2024-11-21 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42204939
- [LYC] Launch YC: Fresco, the scribe for construction, 2024-10-23 — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/M73-fresco-the-scribe-for-construction
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/fresco (now "AI-powered takeoff and estimating for Division 8 construction")
- [KOE] A contractor's daily-log expectations on Procore's support site — https://support.procore.com/tc/Koester/Site_Map/Koester_Expectations_-_Daily_Logs
- [SWI] Swiftask, Procore daily reports page (vendor) — https://swiftask.ai/ai-integration/procore/intelligent-daily-reports
- [BLS] BLS Occupational Outlook, construction managers — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/management/construction-managers.htm
- [OPU] Launch HN: Opusense (field reports for site inspectors), 2025-05-20 — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Construction superintendents on commercial jobs.
   [HN] "Superintendents are the busiest and most expensive people on construction sites."
   [LYC] "That’s the reality for 210k+ construction superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.) across the USA."
   → `roles[superintendent]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: "on commercial jobs" (the founders ask
   for introductions to commercial general contractors in [LYC]).

2. **What (the job).** Keep the record of the day's work, for liability and disputes.
   [HN] "30-200 photos per day to document site progress (mostly for liability reasons, or in case of a dispute with the
   owner over delays and deliverables)"; photos used to create "daily logs", "structured documents that account for the
   work done on site on any given day". [KOE] the log is "a critical piece of documentation in the arbitration of a
   dispute". → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At the end of the day, after the site walks, in the trailer.
   [HN] "At the end of the day, they'll spend a few hours uploading those photos into OneDrive, or project management
   software like Procore or ACC." [YCP] "We were curious what superintendents were doing for hours in their trailers at
   the end of the day." [LYC] "supes are spending up to 3 hours a day creating documents". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: daily log`.
   Author's choice: the recall window {5, WORKING_DAYS} and Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5 (the posts say "per
   day"; a five-day site week is assumed). Prevalence `p_80_100` ("Nearly all") follows from the same "per day".

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** Superintendents at US general contractors whose jobs run on Procore or ACC.
   [LYC] "210k+ construction superintendents ... across the USA"; "Project management tools like Procore and ACC have
   dramatically increased documentation requirements". [YCP] "driving to Napa, South Bay, and around SF". → `context.segment`,
   `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The general contractor, per site.
   [HN] "we charge per site per month, which includes unlimited users on any given construction project".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: contractor}`, the BUYER role. Author's choice: the decider is the contractor's
   "operations lead" and the role to test is "The CFO" (a second role, "The project executive", listed); Purchase
   friction's three steps ("A trial on one live job" tested, a Procore check, a security review) and Commitment's step
   "start a paid pilot on one site" are the author's. Public material names no buyer title; [LYC] asks for
   introductions to general contractors by firm, not by role.

6. **Mechanism.** Narrated short videos turned into notes, texted to the crew, pushed to Procore/ACC.
   [HN] "Supers simply take short videos with voiceover, or upload photos, and Fresco does the rest, creating notes with
   transcription, photos, assignees, and due dates. Supers can easily text their crew action items, and receive texts
   back". "We also route this to whatever project management software they're using with a single click."
   [LYC] the narrated example "The beam in the southwest corner of room 134 is corroded and needs replacement by Alex.";
   "Supes who use Fresco complete their notes, on average, 90% faster."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, Compatibility and Adoption friction items. Relative advantage's two
   benefits are from [HN] ("during their site walks, not after") and [LYC] ("90% faster"); their wording is the author's.

7. **Price.** About $1k per site per month, less with multi-site or multi-month terms.
   [HN] "The typical price is $1k/month, but we offer discounts for multi-month or multi-site commitments."
   → `commercial.price` {800, 1000, month}. Author's choice: the low end of $800 stands for the stated discounts.
   Existing sacrifice: 30 to 60 hours a month per site at an hourly rate of 55 — from [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" and
   [HN] "a few hours uploading", taken as 1.5 to 3 hours on about twenty working days (author's arithmetic). The rate is
   [BLS] "$55.28 per hour" (median, construction managers, May 2025), the author's stand-in: no superintendent wage is
   in the public material. Ability to pay is derived by code (24% to 61%).

8. **Occasions.** The narrated beam; a school refit report; the uploads and logs at the end of the day.
   [LYC] on a school refit walkthrough: "Normally, creating the final report takes 2+ hours."
   [HN] "few supers have time to do this thoroughly, so these photos aren't very searchable." No named customer quote
   exists in public; the occasions below are scripted from these and from practitioner comments.

## Respondents → the public account each story is based on

Superintendents (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):

- Ray Villanueva → [OPU] a former site inspector: "try to remember everything you wanted to write. Sometimes you'd fill in gaps from memory" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44042791 ; delays and weather in the log from [KOE]

- Dwayne Hollis → [LYC] the group is "superintendents (or supervisors, foremen, PMs, etc.)": an assistant super writes the log (the Current-solution escape). Author's invention beyond that.

Contractor operations leads (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Renee Castillo → [HN] the price as offered and "unlimited users"; author's invention for the picks.
- Bill Ostrowski → the price-sceptic comment: "$1k is like way way way out of the reasonable range", "a fraction (e.g. 10%)" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42215232
- Faith Nakamura → author's invention, filling a gap: supers do the logs on their own time, so the firm counts no cost.
- Gordon Achebe → [LYC] "up to 3 hours a day" on a large job; author's invention for the picks.
- Sandra Whitfield → the same price-sceptic comment ("cheaper to get them to do it than buy software at $12k p.a.") — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42215232
- Omar Haddadin → author's invention, filling a gap: a buyer who cannot recall the cost or the budget source (both escapes).
- Lena Brandt → the AEC engineer's comment that integration with existing products drives buying — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44043729 ; author's invention for the picks.
- Trevor McAllister → author's invention, filling a gap: a firm paying a part-time document controller (an amount, not hours).

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds on how often but people
  disagree on whether the log is one of their two worst difficulties; the solution splits on the benefit and on
  talking over videos on site; the price fails (two of eight at the founder's band or above) while the cost it would
  replace is above the price. This is the author's reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- No public account names a buyer title at a general contractor; the decider, the tested role "The CFO", the purchase
  steps and the Commitment step are the author's.
- hourly_rate 55 is a proxy (construction managers, not superintendents).
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are the monthly figures times three.
- The window {5, WORKING_DAYS} is the author's; the public posts say "per day".

insights.line: What made the others more pressing?

whys.g1: Both answers say the schedule and subs no-showing is what outranks the log, so one group named "Schedule and subs not showing up" is exactly how a super would file them, and the name is plain.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing junk sits in the group.

founder.order_why: The look-back window (screen 4) sits between two identical context screens (3 and 5), so I define the context, set the window, then get sent back to the context again, when the window should come after the context is done.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 (same kicker and question: 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.')
founder.missing: Who pays: the superintendent is the user but the general contractor buys per site, and the flow never asks for the buyer or the buyer's role before sending interviews. It also never asks for my solution (narrated site-walk videos turned into notes and pushed to Procore/ACC) or my price (about $1k per site per month), so nothing beyond the problem gets tested.

PRIMARY.order_why: It goes from whether my jobs are on Procore or ACC, to whether and how often I did the log after walks, to what I'd want easier, to the photo upload, which is how my day actually runs, though the first two screens both say 1 of 4.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 2 and 3 overlap a little, since 'did you' and then 'on how many days' could be one question, but it isn't really asked twice.
PRIMARY.missing: How long the log and the photo uploads took me that day (it's hours, not minutes), and whether I've had to pull old logs and photos back up later, like in a delay dispute with the owner, which is why I care that the record is accurate.

screens.why1: Naming the project is the obvious first step of the founder flow, before any study content is asked.
screens.why2: "What should we call this project?" is plain to any founder on first reading.
screens.why3: The founder knows their own product name and tagline, so it is answerable from what I know.
screens.why4: A free-text box with no options, rows or chips.
screens.why5: The typed name "Fresco — the scribe for construction superintendents" keeps my launch words ("the scribe for construction") and my customer (superintendents), so nothing drifted.

screens.why1: Right after naming the project, asking where I sell is the obvious next setup step before any study questions.
screens.why2: "Where are the people who would buy this?" is plain to me; I sell to US general contractors and know that at once.
screens.why3: I know exactly where my buyers are: US GCs, the Bay Area first, Procore and ACC shops.
screens.why4: A country pick with an optional region fits; US with no region is my true answer and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps my answer, the US, unchanged, and "the people who would buy this" matches my buyer being the contractor rather than the super.

screens.why1: Pinning down who, what job, when and which group is the obvious first step before any belief is tested, and it comes right after naming the project and saying where I sell.
screens.why2: Superintendent, site walks, daily log, Procore, ACC and general contractor are my trade's everyday words, and the intro's 'a phrase each' tells me exactly what to type.
screens.why3: These are my own customers and the end-of-day trailer routine I built Fresco around, so I can fill every box from what I know.
screens.why4: The screen shows only boxes to type in and a read-back, with no options, chips or rows to judge.
screens.why5: The read-back keeps my actor, job, circumstance and segment as I meant them and quietly fixes my typos (rcord, photoss, dailyy, generall) without changing the meaning.

screens.why1: Once Keel knows who, what and when, the window comes next: it sets which daily logs a super would actually remember, so it belongs here in the context step.

screens.why3: I know how often my supers do the log, every working day, so I can pick a window from what I know.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 counted', but the line names only Frequency when three beliefs are short, and the deciding '5 needed' appears only down on the cards, so I have to scroll to see why 4 isn't enough.
screens.why_b2: The tally (1 holding, 3 too few, 7 answered) and each card's 'X of 7 · bar · at the bar' or '4 counted · 5 needed' tell me what was counted, over how many and where my bar sits on first read.
screens.why_b3: Prevalence, Frequency, Importance and Current solution carry the exact belief lines I checked, down to the 'five things that are hard' wording and 'uploading site photos and typing the daily log in the trailer'.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do with three of four problem beliefs uncalled: whether to send the study to more supers, how many more, or whether the one holding belief is enough to keep going; 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is stated everywhere, the 4-counted beliefs are refused a call rather than spun, and Prevalence is reported as 'at the bar' rather than strong.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only 4 of 7 supers were counted on Frequency, Importance and Current solution, and each needs 5. Get at least 1 to 3 more superintendents who did a daily log this week before reading whether the log is their worst pain; Prevalence holds at 6 of 7.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the deciding number, '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7 · at the bar', so I know it held and by exactly how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip reads at a glance: 7 cells on a 0 to 7 axis, 6 for and 1 against, with my bar marked at 6 and labelled 'at least 8 in 10'.
screens.why_b3: I recognise my belief, but 'did their daily log after site walks' loses my 'on commercial jobs' and turns my problem (typing the log up in the trailer after the walks) into simply doing a log, which every working super does.
screens.why_b4: The So line sends me to the next two cards, but it doesn't say what this means for Fresco, such as that one more No would have flipped it or that a Yes here doesn't yet mean the log is costing them hours.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and 'a lean, not a call' is said, but 'Holding up' rests on a gate that counts any super who did a log at all: Denise, who finishes hers as she goes, counts for me, and the only No is Jolene, who was between jobs, so nobody whose log already works could say No; the '— the most recent time it happened' tag on a yes/no question also reads oddly.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of my 7 supers had the daily log still to do after their site walks, exactly my bar for 8 in 10, so one more No would have sunk it; this tells me the log is everyday, not that it costs hours, so read How often and Importance before trusting it.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside "4 counted · 5 needed to call it", so I know there is no verdict and exactly why.
screens.why_b2: The days axis and the strip are clear, but it took me a second look to tell apart the two bars: my 4-to-5-days range on the chart, and the "your bar · 4 of 5 (at least 2 in 3)" people marker on the strip. The chart also starts at 0 when nobody could answer 0.
screens.why_b3: Frequency is the right name, and "do their daily log after site walks on 4 to 5 working days out of 5" is recognisably my belief, but it drops "on commercial jobs" and rewords the end-of-day upload I described.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is generic: it doesn't tell me that all four counted answers are for me, or that one more countable answer at 4 or 5 days would make it hold.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (6 answered, 4 counted), Hank and Luis are excluded with reasons, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" claims nothing beyond the data, though the stray "the most recent time it happened" tag on a count question is odd.
screens.instead: Too few to call: all 4 counted said 4 or 5 days (middle answer 5), so it leans your way; one more countable answer at 4 or 5 days and it holds.

screens.why_b1: The status *Too few to call* sits right beside its number, *4 counted · 5 needed to call it*, and the So line repeats both, so I know where I stand and why.
screens.why_b2: The caption says it plainly: 4 people, two picks each, bars count the 8 picks; my row is marked *the problem you named* with its 2, and the strip shows one cell per person with the bar at 4 of 5.
screens.why_b3: The title is Importance and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, with *Logging the day's photos and notes* as my own row.
screens.why_b4: *Nothing is settled here yet* is generic: it doesn't say that schedule and subs out-picked my log 3 to 2, or that even one more *for* at five would only make 3 of 5, under the bar of 4.
screens.why_b5: n and the low count are visible, but *a lean, not a call* suggests a direction that a 2-for, 2-against split doesn't have.
screens.instead: 2 of 4 put the log in their two, and schedule and subs were picked more often (3 each); one more for still makes only 3 of 5, under the bar, so ask more supers before you lead with the log.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both, so I know why there is no call.
screens.why_b2: The rungs with their for and against counts and the line under 'Done in the trailer in under an hour' read at once, but the strip's 'your bar · 4 of 5' with a ghost cell, while 6 answered and 4 were counted, took me a second look to see that it means 4 of a 5-person floor, not 4 of my 4.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Current solution', the belief about uploading site photos and typing the daily log in the trailer, and the bar rung 'Done in the trailer in under an hour' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic: it doesn't tell me that 3 of my 4 counted supers already fell short, or that one more counted answer at or below my line would decide it, so I don't know whether to chase one more super.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Hank and Luis are named as not counted with their reasons, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps 3 of 4 from being sold as a result.
screens.instead: Say: 3 of 4 counted took hours or finished at home, 1 logged on site; one more counted super decides it, so get one more answer and ask about the log itself, not just the photo upload.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Too few to call' sits right beside '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', so I know there is no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: The box is named Importance and carries my belief word for word as I checked it on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen tells me what to do next: not to get one more superintendent through, not what the schedule-and-subs pull means for pitching the log as the pain, and not why my Current solution belief has no box here at all.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible ('2 against · 2 asked their why here', the group's 2), the low n is said in the status line, and nothing is called strong.
screens.why_b6: Ray's 'the log can wait till morning, the deck can't' and Denise finishing hers on the tablet before the gate tell me something I did not type: the log is a deferrable chore that loses to schedule and subs, so time saved may not be what makes a super care.

screens.why1: A first-screen check that my jobs actually run on Procore or ACC is the obvious gate for a study about getting the day's photos and notes into the daily log.
screens.why2: Procore and ACC are the platforms I log into every day, so the question reads plain on first pass.
screens.why3: I know exactly which of my current jobs are set up in which platform, so I can answer it straight.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it cleanly, with no overlap and nothing missing for a gate.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment (GCs whose jobs run on Procore or ACC) and leaks nothing of the product or any founder language.
screens.why6: It says well overall, but ACC is an abbreviation that would usually be said as letters, and 'I'll read 2 options' is clunky where 'Yes or no' would do for a screener.
screens.instead: Are any of the jobs you're running now set up in Procore or Autodesk Construction Cloud? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking if my jobs are on Procore or ACC, asking about my daily log this week is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: Daily log and site walks are my words, and I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I do the daily log every working day, so I know straight away whether I did it this week.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and the chips beside them belong to the story box after a Yes, not to this question.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but 'do your daily log' has lost the founder's 'type up', which is the part that made it a problem, so the meaning has drifted.
screens.why6: One short sentence then 'Yes or no.', easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: Every super does the daily log after the walks, so this asks the circumstance and not the problem: everyone says Yes, nobody can truly say No, and the belief can never be refuted, like the card's bad example.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you type up the daily log after your site walks? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after I said yes, I did my log after the walks, asking on how many of the five days is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Daily log" and "site walks" are my words, but "did your daily log after site walks" made me read it twice, since the log gets done every day and I wasn't sure whether "after" was the point or just the timing.
screens.why3: I know exactly which days this week I sat down and did the log, so I can answer from memory.
screens.why4: One button per working day from 1 to 5 covers every true answer, none overlap, and I can't recall sits apart as the only escape.
screens.why5: The founder's situation is the photos and notes still waiting to go into the log, but this asks only whether I did the log, which on a commercial job is every day, so the part that eats my evening has dropped out.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and "a number from 1 to 5, or say you can't recall" is easy to hold and answer once heard.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of working days out of 5, from 1 up to the window's 5, with the one escape apart and no 0, so a founder's low of 2 or more can be held or refuted, though nearly every super will say 5.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, on how many days did you have to get your site photos and notes into the daily log after your walks? 1 · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 · I can't recall

screens.why1: After three screens about doing my daily log after site walks, asking what part of my day I'd most like made easier is an obvious next step.
screens.why2: Subs, RFIs, submittals and the daily log's photos and notes are my everyday words, and I'd answer this on first read.
screens.why3: Every one of these is something I deal with myself on my jobs, so I can answer from my last day on site.
screens.why4: Getting subs to show up and finish is a big part of why a job falls behind, so it overlaps with keeping the job on schedule, and both are whole-job worries rather than one thing I do that day.
screens.why5: Logging the day's photos and notes keeps the founder's daily-log record in my words, and nothing about a product or the company reaches me.
screens.why6: Five short options, one question and one escape at the end, all easy to hold by ear.
screens.why7: The own item is there and not first, there are five options with None of these at the first ask, and the belief can go either way, but the rivals drift from the end-of-day logging moment into whole-job aims (safety, schedule) and one is a cause of another, which bends the rival rule and stacks the picks against the own row.
screens.instead: Think of your last day on site. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Logging the day's photos and notes · Updating the three-week look-ahead · Writing up the day's delays for the PM · Tracking the day's manpower and deliveries · Chasing RFIs and submittals · None of these

screens.why1: Right after asking what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last daily log actually went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Every word is plain to me, but the question asks about uploading photos and the answers are about when and where the log got done, so I'd have to read it twice to work out which one I'm answering.
screens.why3: I upload my own site photos and write my own daily log, so I know exactly how my last one went.
screens.why4: None of the five answers how the photo upload went; my true answer, 'took a few hours to get them all into Procore', isn't there; 'Log done on site' is a place where the others are times; and 'at home or the next morning' joins two cases.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks to me, but the founder's pain was the hours spent uploading photos, and the options have drifted to when the log was finished.
screens.why6: Short stem and five short options I can hold in my head when it's read out, with the one escape said last.
screens.why7: The rungs grade a stand-in, when and where the log was finished, mixed with place, instead of the time the upload took, so they can't answer whether uploading photos still falls short; the first rung works and the last fails, but the measure is the wrong one.
screens.instead: Think of your last daily log. How long did getting the day's site photos uploaded take? Under 15 minutes · About half an hour · About an hour · A couple of hours or more · Never got them all uploaded; escape: Someone else did it.
